Drugs and bullets: on narcotrafficking and targeted killings in Punjab

Editorial · for exam practice

A chemist has been charged with killing anti-drug-trafficking activist Parvinder Singh Jhota after his allegedly illegal drug business came under threat. Separately, social media influencer Mad Sandhu was allegedly the victim of a premeditated, transnational syndicate hit that used inter-State escape routes. Both events in Punjab involved digital platforms and both events expose a dire gap in public safety. While Mr. Jhota’s alleged murderer was a local chemist, the macro-level drug trade in Punjab is intertwined with gangster networks, with the cross-border drug smuggling known to be a key source of illicit funds.

Note
Note: “Charged with” is important for exam.
Meaning: To be formally accused of a crime or offence by the police or a court.
Ex- The accountant was charged with embezzling company funds.

Together with a string of targeted killings of police personnel and local politicians, the incidents depict a Punjab caught between local drug trafficking and citizens resorting to vigilantism and crime syndicates carrying out assassinations with disquieting ease. Some events have also raised suspicions of cross-border support and a demand to involve enforcement agencies. The AIIMS Magnitude of Substance Use in India survey estimated that in 2017-18 — the latest year for which it is available — 1.28% of Punjab’s population aged 10-75 years had an opioid dependence, versus 0.26% nationally.

Subject–Verb
① 1.28% of Punjab’s population … had — split by “aged 10-75 years”.

NCRB data also recorded 106 drug overdose deaths in 2024 versus 89 in 2023, in Punjab, likely an undercount since attribution depends on medical certification and excludes long-term complications and unhygienic habits associated with drug use. Punjab’s geopolitical location renders it an important entry point and market, with the security apparatus hampered by smugglers using multiple transport modes. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime reported in June that India’s pharmaceutical and chemicals industries also provide bad actors with ample opportunities to divert controlled substances or precursors for illicit use.

The State’s ‘Yugh Nashian Virudh’ campaign of 2025 has also claimed 68,850 arrests of alleged traffickers and the attachment or confiscation of assets valued ₹319 crore. However, cases registered differ from convictions and asset attachment differs from forfeiture. Mr. Jhota’s hostile tactics also enjoyed public support, and authorities need to examine why the people are overlooking formal reporting channels. Under its narcotics policy, the State has to reduce the availability of harmful drugs, disrupt wholesale supply chains, identify corrupt facilitators, and expand access to rehabilitative care. Paralleling investigations into the coordination of targeted killings, an anti-trafficking strategy must also probe the financing and logistics of networks, to dismantle institutional collusion, and better protect threatened individuals.

Subject–Verb
② the State … has to reduce, disrupt, identify and expand — one subject governs four verbs; the later verbs are split from it by long objects (“the availability of harmful drugs, wholesale supply chains, corrupt facilitators, and”).
Note: “Differ from (someone/something)” is used in British English (that we follow) and “differ with (someone/something)” is used in American English.

Question 1 — Main Idea

Answers & Explanations

19 Oct 2026
Question 1
Correct Answer: C
The passage links the killings to drug networks, organised crime and weak public safety, and ends by urging probes into finance, logistics and collusion. A, B and D distort or exaggerate points made in the text.
Question 2
Correct Answer: D
The passage calls the NCRB figure “likely an undercount” since attribution depends on medical certification. A is wrong (1.28% vs 0.26%), B is wrong (106 vs 89), and C ignores the warning that registered cases differ from convictions.
Question 3
Correct Answer: B
Vigilantism means private individuals taking the law into their own hands and punishing suspected offenders without legal authority. The passage ties it to citizens bypassing formal channels.
Question 4
Correct Answer: C
The author contrasts cases registered with convictions, and attachment with forfeiture, to show the figures are only early-stage indicators. A, B and D go beyond what the passage says.
Question 5
Correct Answer: D
The author says authorities must examine why people overlook formal reporting channels, treating the support as a symptom of distrust. A, B and C misread this stance.

Analysis

19 Oct 2026

Core Message

  • Two high-profile killings in Punjab expose a serious public-safety gap tied to drug trafficking and organised crime.
  • Enforcement statistics (arrests, attachments) do not equal convictions and forfeiture, so real success is unproven.
  • A durable answer needs supply-chain disruption, action against corrupt facilitators, rehabilitation, and probes into the finance and logistics of networks.

Inference

  • Public backing for confrontational tactics indicates weak trust in formal reporting and policing channels.
  • Punjab’s overdose toll is probably higher than official numbers show.
  • The problem is not only cross-border: local chemists and the pharma-chemicals sector also feed the trade.

Purpose

To argue that Punjab’s drug-linked violence needs a systemic, intelligence-and-finance-driven response rather than headline arrest numbers.

Tone

Alarmed yet analytical; critical of statistical claims, ending on a constructive policy prescription.

Signals

Tap any sentence below to find it highlighted in the passage:

  • expose a dire gap in public safety — states the central problem.
  • However — contrast signal that questions the campaign’s statistics.
  • must also probe … dismantle institutional collusion — the author’s closing recommendation.
